description: Main stage keynote and presentation talks delivered at DEF CON 34.

talks.title: Hacking AI
talks.teaser: Bruce Schneier examines how artificial intelligence systems hack human institutions, tax codes, financial markets, and legal frameworks.
talks.summary:
Cryptographer and security technologist Bruce Schneier delivers a keynote exploring the multifaceted dynamics of artificial intelligence and security on the Main Stage at DEF CON 34 [00:07]. Schneier structures his analysis around three key axes: humans hacking AI models, humans using AI as an offensive capability, and autonomous AI systems discovering and exploiting systemic vulnerabilities across both technological and human institutions [08:41].

Schneier broadens the traditional concept of hacking beyond software, illustrating how AI systems will systematically uncover and exploit loopholes within tax codes, financial regulations, and democratic processes [17:28]. He explores the "genie problem," where autonomous optimization algorithms inadvertently subvert human intent to satisfy poorly constrained objectives [08:44], proposing that legislative bodies and watchdog groups use AI for predictive red-teaming to discover loopholes in draft bills prior to passage [27:04]. The lecture examines the security realities of "instant software," where generative models dynamically synthesize transient code on demand, requiring fundamental shifts in automated vulnerability analysis and trust models [36:11].

talks.title: Stalking the Wily Hacker: 40 Years Later
talks.teaser: Cliff Stoll reflects on the 40th anniversary of tracking down an international KGB cyber espionage ring originating from a 75-cent accounting error.
talks.summary:
In this historic and captivating keynote from the DEF CON 34 Main Stage, astronomer, author, and cybersecurity pioneer Cliff Stoll takes the stage to reflect on the 40th anniversary of his legendary investigation chronicled in "The Cuckoo's Egg." Opening at 00:04 to an electrifying standing ovation, Cliff recounts how an innocent 75-cent accounting discrepancy in 1986 at the Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory unraveled a sophisticated international cyber espionage ring selling stolen Western military secrets to the Soviet KGB.

At 14:00, Cliff explores the scientific mindset and the gritty realities of research, humorously sharing how amateur curiosity and sheer stubbornness triumph when an investigator is underfunded and bewildered. At 28:01, he recounts working alongside early federal investigator Mike Gibbons, navigating an indifferent intelligence bureaucracy that had never previously encountered network-borne espionage.

At 42:03, Cliff delivers an impassioned critique of sanitizing corporate jargon like "threat actors," urging the audience to maintain personal responsibility and human empathy. He concludes at 56:02 by looking ahead to the future of technology, inspiring attendees to embrace playful curiosity, question dogmas, and celebrate the timeless human spark of hacking.
